title: The Quiet Years
blurb: 1988–2006. Classical machine learning, done justice. At Bell Labs a pierced stencil learns ZIP codes from Buffalo's mail and later reads cheques by the million: a winter of prestige, not of use. Statistics beat hand-written rules in speech and translation, forests of decision trees vote, and the support vector machine offers the widest street and one clean bowl with a proof at the bottom. A candle is lit for 'fiddly, and beaten anyway', with a few stubborn holdouts at its rim, among them Hinton, LeCun and Bengio; a dinner bet is signed; the messenger's whisper fades and a protected pipe carries it; a chess machine wins twenty-nine years late. So why would anyone choose the fog?

shots.setting: Holmdel, New Jersey · 1988–1989 · night · a Bell Labs lab bench under a desk lamp
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Bell Labs, 1989: a pierced tin stencil slides over a handwritten digit as LeCun's net learns to read ZIP codes, and a mail sack from Buffalo spills onto the bench. CHAPTER INDEX TAB (the film's chapter-card device for clue chapters): at the shot's first frame a manila index tab, typed in Special Elite with the chapter title 'The Quiet Years', drops down from the frame's top edge at top-left, like a file-divider tab, holds for 2.5 seconds over the picture, and slides back up; no new shot, no lamp change. The picture fades up from black in duskRose; the tab rides over the first line. Establishing beat: a vast low building of mirrored glass at dusk, a whole sky reflected in it (no logos, no signage). Inside, a lab bench: a beige PC, a small video camera on a gooseneck stand bent over a handwritten digit under a desk lamp, a CRT glowing beside it. A man (LeCun) leans in at the bench, standing. Teaching machine, brief preview: stencilLantern. The digit on the bench becomes the stitched tapestry '4'; a small 3×3 pierced tin lantern (kernel 'vertical') slides across it for the first dozen positions, and the wall beside the bench fills the first row of the feature map, cell by cell, in raster order; showKernel off, showSum off (the full mechanics belong to chapter 8). On the CRT, the recognised digit appears in phosphor. On 'Buffalo', a canvas mail sack slumps onto the bench, stencilled BUFFALO, N.Y., and envelopes with handwritten ZIP codes slide out. Just after the line, wordless (the aside 'Buffalo, again' was cut in round 8; the picture keeps the rhyme), a ghost of chapter 3's typewriter date stamp, BUFFALO · 1958–60 (the same stamp used in ch03-s04, ch08-s03 and ch15-s08), prints itself faintly over the sack and then fades, and for a moment a faint ghost of the Mark I's silhouette (chapter 3's knob machine) shows in the post-office window behind the sack: the case keeps passing through the same city. Numbers on screen only.

shots.setting: a bank's back room · late 1990s · night · a cheque sorter running; snow on a lecture hall across the street
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a bank's cheque sorter runs warm, a stencil flashing over every amount, while across the street snow lies on a dark lecture hall: used, not admired. A bank's back room at night, lit warm: a long cheque-sorting machine, belts and rollers in silhouette, cheques flicking through one after another like playing cards. Above the rollers a tiny stencil lantern (the same one from shot 1) flashes over the handwritten amount on each cheque as it passes, and the amount appears in clean type on a small display. Date stamp in IBM Plex Mono: 1998. The quote card rises over the machine. Then the camera drifts to the window: across the street, a grand lecture hall with tall dark windows stands under falling snow, its lamps out and a single noticeboard frosted over. Inside the bank, the machine keeps running, warm. The image holds both at once: the cold outside is about prestige; the work inside never stopped. Small label (set in just after 'winter', as the drift to the window begins, low in frame, riding the drift back inside): fielded from 1996, and at work on about one US cheque in ten, by LeCun's estimate; it holds through the music-only hold so it can be read in silence. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. SCRIPT NOTE (review round 1): the quote card is verbatim US spelling from the 1998 abstract: 'reads several million checks per day' (not 'cheques').

shots.setting: the rivals' gallery, then Vapnik's blackboard · 1987–2001 · evening · statistics over rules, forests that vote; the widest street between two crowds; then one clean bowl beside the misty hills
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the rivals' gallery unrolls (statistics pairing translations, forests of trees voting), then Vapnik opens the widest street between two crowds and the plate tilts into one clean bowl. Opening: a short paper strip unrolls across the stage, the rivals' gallery, played in the spoken order. On 'translation': a parchment of two bilingual columns (English and French, the Canadian parliament's record; text is texture only), threads of light pairing line to line, while a small hand-cut rulebook beside it is set aside, closed (statistics learned from data over hand-written rules). On 'Forests': a little forest of cut-paper decision trees, each tree a few branching cuts, each raising a tiny paper flag; the majority colour wins. On 'Vapnik's' the strip rolls aside onto the favourite. A blackboard (Vapnik, stocky, chalk in hand; name card crediting his collaborators Cortes, Guyon and Boser) with two crowds of dots. The board becomes a paper-cut street scene: two crowds of small paper lanterns, warm on the left, cool on the right, and between them the widest possible empty street, with a lit centre line. The few lanterns standing right on each kerb glow brighter and get small chalk circles (the support vectors; drawn, not labelled). A narrower street is tried first (faint, wrong, then erased) so the 'widest' reads as a choice. The margin equation inks onto the board margin. On 'landscape', the street plate tilts away and becomes a side-on paper landscape (the mistyHills kit with a convex loss: lossF(x) = x², no fog; KIT WORK, blocking: mistyHills {lossF, lossDf, minima} per staging.kitWork): ONE CLEAN BOWL, smooth, no ridges. A ball of light set anywhere on its rim rolls straight to the single bottom (do it twice from opposite sides; both reach the same point). Beside it, smaller and to the right, chapter 5's misty hills return in miniature, fog and hollow and all, the timid traveller still stuck. On 'with a proof', a small parchment tag pins to the bowl's floor: 'one global optimum'. This is the fairest case for the age's belief: present it with real admiration. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The strip's two panels are pictures, not text items (no captions). (Breiman's 2001 SVM sentence, and his concession that a hand-built net beat his forest on ZIP codes, move to the end-credits sources card.)

shots.setting: Vapnik's blackboard turned workbench · 1992–2012 · evening · the classical recipe as a two-stage machine: hand-cut features, then a simple learner; the kernel trick lifts two crowds onto a hill
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the classical recipe staged as a two-stage paper machine, so the viewer sees what 'clean learning, hand-made seeing' means. CAMERA: a slow lateral track left to right along a workbench below Vapnik's blackboard (same duskRose as ch06-s03), then a gentle rise for the lift. STAGE ONE, on 'expert': a pair of hands (an expert's, shirt-sleeved; not the narrator's tweed cuffs) cuts a small TIN STENCIL with snips: a few hand-chosen shapes (an edge, a corner, a loop), the same kind of pierced stencil that returns in ch08-s04 (rhyme it: same tin, same pierced dots); each photo slid under the stencil becomes a short row of numbers. STAGE TWO, on 'line': a simple learner (a small brass ruler on a pivot) swings over a field of paper dots, warm on one side, cool on the other, and settles on one straight chalk line between them. On 'kernel': the two crowds are mixed so no straight line can part them (a warm ring around a cool cluster, flat on the board); the date card sets in (1992 · Boser, Guyon & Vapnik). On 'lifted': the board's paper plane rises into a gentle HILL (the warm ring stays low on the slopes, the cool cluster rides up to the summit), side-lit so the height reads. On 'flat cut': one flat sheet of vellum slides in horizontally and slices the hill between them: one flat cut parts the crowds; drop back down to the flat board and the cut becomes a closed chalk ring around the cool cluster. On 'clean': the brass ruler and the vellum sheet glow softly (the learning: tidy, provable). On 'hand-made': the camera settles back on the expert's tin stencil at the left of the bench, snips beside it, lamp-lit: the seeing was cut by hand. Hold on it. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot: the date card and the term label 'kernel trick'. SCRIPT NOTE (review round 9): the recipe is now two lines, using the old silent tail: L0607b (the expert's stencil, the ruler's line) and L0607c (the kernel lift and flat cut; 'clean' and 'hand-made'); the beats keep their words.

shots.setting: the study candle shelf, then the candle stage · late 1990s to 2004 · night · the quiet-years candle; a few stubborn holdouts at the rim, three of them named: Toronto, Holmdel, Montréal
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the quiet-years candle is lit for the age's verdict on nets, and at its rim three small holdouts lift their hand-lanterns: Hinton, LeCun and Bengio. CAMERA: SHELF (low macro; the candle lit), then the flame push onto the stage. Cut to the candle shelf below the case board, with crossfadeMood duskRose→candleAmber, 0.7 s, no dip, under the cut (so the previous plate's duskRose does not pop to the study's candleAmber), settling into the study's candleAmber. The hands light a new candle: NEURAL NETS ARE FIDDLY, AND BEATEN ANYWAY (small caps, IBM Plex Mono era face). CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Here the candle is new: no sleeve yet, only the full stub with its flame at the top ring. On 'candle' push into the flame onto the stage (the push-into-the-flame cue, done in-shot), tint-crossfading (crossfadeMood) from candleAmber to duskRose as the camera passes through the flame; on the stage the candle stands huge and casts a wide duskRose pool. Inside the pool, facing the flame: a large, comfortable crowd of generic silhouettes (conference-goers, reviewers with stacks of papers, a whiteboard showing the clean bowl). At the rim, half in shadow and facing out, long shadows across the floor, a few small figures each holding a small hand-lantern, spaced far apart along the dark edge. Most stay unnamed and faint (the circle was wider than three: the bible's holdouts include Bottou, Hochreiter, Schmidhuber and the CIFAR circle; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber get their own shot next). Three are nearer the camera, each at their own place in the dark: LeCun standing (stamp HOLMDEL / NEW YORK); the tall man SEATED at a desk by a Toronto window (Hinton, seated, never standing in this era; stamp TORONTO); and Bengio standing (stamp MONTRÉAL). Each hand-lantern lifts as its owner is named, in the spoken order: Hinton's (seated), then LeCun's, then Bengio's; each name card appears with its lift. These three are the film's named holdouts who return at the rim in later chapters, never presented as the only ones. During the hold: a thin thread of light runs between the hand-lanterns through the dark, the three named ones and two of the fainter ones (one of them Fleet's, unnamed on screen but for the label), with the label '2004 · CIFAR's NCAP: Hinton, Bengio, Fleet and others'; the joined hand-lanterns brighten slightly. The thread starts as LeCun's quoted words begin ('We couldn't get our papers published' is said of exactly this circle, which 'gave us a place where we could exchange ideas'), so the label has the rest of the line and the whole hold to be read. The big pool does not notice. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The spoken LeCun quote needs no card; the stamps HOLMDEL / NEW YORK, TORONTO and MONTRÉAL are place stamps, not text items; the Bengio and Hinton testimony and LeCun's 'conspiracy' phrase move to the end-credits sources card. STUDY LOCK (staging rule): every beat in the study, at the case board, on the candle shelf or at the Wall of Forecasts is candleAmber; era colour enters the study only through practicals (the window's sky, a glowing prop); a shot that crosses between the study and a stage or era location tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood) at the moment it crosses, and the shot's mood field names its opening location.

shots.setting: Bell Labs, Holmdel · 14 March 1995 · evening · one typed sheet on a table; then a restaurant table
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: top-down on the typed 1995 bet sheet: two wagers, three signatures, and the question card WHO PAID FOR DINNER? pinned on the oxblood thread. CAMERA: top-down on the bet sheet at Bell Labs (era location), then BOARD (the Q2 pin as an insert). Top-down: one typed sheet on a table under a lamp, two numbered bets separated by a row of asterisks. The camera reads it the way a detective reads a document, panning slowly line by line; the typed text is texture, not to be read, except the phrase the narrator speaks: first Jackel's bet (on 'One' a soft lamp glow passes over its line (his name appears only on the one combined name card at the signing, never spoken)), then Vapnik's. As the camera reaches Vapnik's bet, the short quote card of that sentence lifts off the sheet (early, so it can be read); on 'no one in his right mind', those words are underlined by the narrator's pen. Three signatures write themselves in at the bottom in sequence, each dated 3/14/95: V. Vapnik, L. Jackel, and 'Witnessed by Y. LeCun'. Side view: three seated silhouettes at a table (Jackel, Vapnik, LeCun), a fountain pen passed hand to hand, two wine glasses set out for the dinners to come. On 'who paid', the study (tint-crossfade, crossfadeMood, from the Bell Labs duskRose to the study's candleAmber as the board comes into frame): the hands pin a new card on the oxblood question-card thread along the top of the case board, WHO PAID FOR DINNER?, in slot Q2 (Q1 burned out in ch05-s06), and it sways a little. The sheet itself is then pinned below the thread (ch07-s01 finds it there), with Vapnik's quote card still on it, so the full sentence stays readable to the end of the shot. lines.text: In 1995, at Bell Labs, two colleagues signed a pair of bets, a fancy dinner each. Larry Jackel bet that by 2000 we would understand why big neural nets work. Vladimir Vapnik bet that by 2005 “no one in his right mind” would use nets like those.

lines.direction: amused, the narrator likes these men; three short sentences, a small breath after each; read the quoted fragment exactly, with a twinkle and no judgement

shots.setting: a long line of lanterns · 1991–1997 · night · a whisper fading; a protected pipe
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a long chain of lanterns: the messenger bead halves at every lantern and fades like a whisper, until a protected pipe carries it at full strength past a thousand steps. Teaching machine: a deep chain built from the lanternNetwork kit: twelve paper lanterns in a long horizontal line on one string, receding in perspective (layers, or the words of a long sentence read one at a time; on 'word by word' a faint word-tag hangs under each lantern for a moment, then fades; on 'sentence' a small warm glow is handed along the string from lantern to lantern, the net's memory of what it has read so far). KIT WORK, blocking: lanternNetwork {topology: custom layer sizes + fixed weights} per staging.kitWork. At the right end, the error glows bright (strength 1.0) and the messenger bead sets off to the left. At each lantern it passes, the bead's ring of light is multiplied by the same factor, 0.5 (a tiny diagram mark on the first lantern, '× 0.5', tagged 'illustrative'), and visibly shrinks; a small readout under each lantern prints its strength: 1 → 0.5 → 0.25 → 0.125 → … By the eighth lantern the bead is a faint speck; by the twelfth (≈ 0.0005) it is gone, and the first lanterns never feel it: a whisper fading down a long line. Label (on the whisper's end): 'vanishing gradients · found by Hochreiter, 1991, and independently by Bengio, Simard & Frasconi, 1994'. Then on 'protected pipe' a second line is drawn below: the same lanterns, but threaded through a straight paper pipe with a self-loop marked '× 1.0' and two small hinged valves (input gate, output gate). The bead enters the pipe and travels the whole length at full brightness, and the camera pulls back as the pipe extends far past the frame, with a counter ticking past 1,000 steps. Hochreiter at the end of the pipe (name card as the names are spoken), standing. No quote card: the narration carries the thousand steps, and the 1997 abstract goes to the end-credits sources card. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. The per-lantern strength readouts and the pipe's '× 1.0' loop mark and two valves are diagram marks of the teaching machine, kept small. Plant: this pipe will meet its replacement in chapter 10.

shots.setting: the Wall of Forecasts beside the case board · May 1997, then the year 2000 · night
shots.visual: THIS SHOT: on the Wall, the yellowed chess slip is unpinned and corrected to 1997, twenty-nine years late, a point for RULES; then a 2000 calendar leaf drifts by and Turing's slip curls. CAMERA: the reverse flame push out to SHELF, then WALL (a short truck to W2), a 1–2 s BOARD insert on the RULES pin, a FILE insert (the slip laid face down), then WALL again for W1. Reverse flame push back to the study (no lamp change, no black): the bead of light in the previous shot's protected pipe becomes a candle flame filling the frame, and the camera pulls back out of the flame of the quiet-years candle onto the study's candle shelf, tint-crossfading (crossfadeMood) from duskRose to candleAmber as it clears the flame; then a short pan from the shelf to the Wall. The study is locked to candleAmber. The Wall of Forecasts, pinned beside the board, in its fixed slot order from the lamp outward: Turing's slip (1950), the chess slip (Simon and Newell, 1958), Rosenblatt's 1961 slip; then empty pin-holes for slips still to come; and toward the dark end, beyond the lamp's pool, one slip hanging in shadow, only its corner half-lit, its text unreadable (the 30-to-50-years slip, planted in ch01-s05, never mentioned here; corner only); the far end beyond it is bare. The chess slip, already yellowed and curled since chapter 4, is in the lamp's pool; its typed prediction is the slip's own text, seen before, not a new card. On 'promised' the slip catches the light as the narrator voices its forecast. On 'came', a small paper-cut vignette plays inside the slip's frame: a quiet wood-panelled room, a chessboard, a player's silhouette leaning back, and behind him two tall black towers (no logos). Date stamp in Plex Mono: NEW YORK · 11 MAY 1997. On 'late' the hands unpin the chess slip and turn it over; on the back the fountain pen writes '1968 → 1997 · 29 years late'. On 'search', a small label: '200 million positions a second' (the narration carries 'no neural network'). On 'Rules', the camera glances to the case board's RULES suspect card (the paper-cut key over a branching tree, ch01-s05 and ch02) and the hands press one brass pin beside it: the first point Rules scores in the film, given fairly. The chess slip is laid face down in the file, leaving its pin empty in its slot. Then, without narration: a calendar leaf reading 2000 drifts down past the Wall, and Turing's slip (the first forecast, 1950; its own typed fragment 'in about fifty years' time' visible as before) curls at its edges as the date passes. It is not taken down. Its pin stays. TEXT RULE: besides stamps and name cards, at most two text items in this shot. STUDY LOCK (staging rule): every beat in the study, at the case board, on the candle shelf or at the Wall of Forecasts is candleAmber; era colour enters the study only through practicals (the window's sky, a glowing prop); a shot that crosses between the study and a stage or era location tint-crossfades (crossfadeMood) at the moment it crosses, and the shot's mood field names its opening location.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a clue card is pinned, the clean bowl catches the light, and the question card WHY WOULD ANYONE CHOOSE THE FOG? is pinned as fog drifts across the board. CAMERA: BOARD (the C2-d pin and the Q3 card as inserts), with one FILE-camera insert (top-down on the desk) for the bowl and the hills. The case board under the green lamp. The hands pin this chapter's clue card into slot C2-d at the foot of column C2, beneath the 1986 bead card in C2-b (the scissors card in C2-a above both): a pierced tin stencil (1989), with a small straight pipe drawn beside it. Threads of light tie it to the bead card and, faintly, to the 1958 knob card in C1-b. Then (still in the lead-in), on the desk in front of the board, two small paper objects are set side by side in the lamp's pool by the hands: the clean bowl from shot 3 (a ball sitting calmly at its single bottom) and a miniature of the misty hills, fog curling, the tiny traveller with his lantern still in the hollow. The shot is silent until the card: the narrator voices its question once (L0616) as it is pinned, and ch08-s13b answers it. First the bowl catches the light (the picture alone says one clean bowl, no fog, no traps); then the hands pin a new card on the oxblood question-card thread along the top of the board, next to WHO PAID FOR DINNER?: WHY WOULD ANYONE CHOOSE THE FOG? Slow push in to the card; as the card settles, the hills' fog drifts across the bowl's edge. In the last seconds of the hold, a wisp of fog drifts in front of the card, and behind it the traveller's lantern, far away, still glows.
